name: Grace Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. We keep your answers confidential. What does an ordinary day at work involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Grace Dubois, 58, and I help patch walls, replace trim and carry materials on a library repair site. I left school early and only recently moved into construction, so I ask the site lead to check my measurements when the old rooms turn crooked. I like solving those small surprises, even if the lower wage and stiff knees make each week a calculation.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because planning could change before I have a stronger work record, and the robots would follow around 2031. Paid training on real equipment, clear references, and actual local vacancies would help me keep earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets paid to find the hidden damage after a perfect schedule is printed. I have lifted enough skirting to know the wall often has its own plan.

headlineQuote: I have lifted enough skirting to know the wall often has its own plan.
portrait: Grace is a **58-year-old junior** construction worker learning repairs on a library site after leaving school early.
She uses **AI daily** for lookup, then checks measurements and advice against manuals or the site lead.
Her **low wage** supports the household while Marc’s shoulder injury makes his driving hours uncertain.
Across the scenarios, she pursues **paid evidence and vacancies** without assuming a safer occupation after robots arrive.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** compresses her chance to build a repair record before robots threaten physical work around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid equipment training**, a clear work reference, and real local vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my crew that the AI voice on my phone saves me hunting through tool catalogues, even if the big claims fade. The AI voice on my phone does not know whether the old plaster will crumble when I lift a skirting board.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a plateau would let me keep doing work I am finally getting better at. I am still on the lower wage, though, and with less than a month saved a delay in the library repair contract would hurt us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid repair shifts and checking measurements with the site lead before I cut anything. During the first year I would cancel the extra streaming subscription and put that payment toward the van insurance bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel relieved about the pace and cross about having to count every small purchase. My partner Marc is recovering from a shoulder injury, so his driving hours have been patchy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you actually ask the phone at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I ask it for a hinge name or the order of steps in a repair, then I compare the answer with the manual or the site lead. I use it most days, but I have seen it invent a screw size.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who relies on your wages now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marc and I pay our own bills; our children are grown and have their own places. When his driving hours dip, my site wage becomes the steady part of the month, small as it is.

say: I would say **AI lookup** helps with catalogues but cannot judge old plaster.
I would remind the crew to **check measurements** before cutting.
think: I welcome a **slower pace** because I am still improving at repair work.
Our **thin cushion** makes any delay to the library contract costly.
do: Keep taking **paid repairs** and confirm measurements with the site lead.
Cancel the **streaming subscription** to cover van insurance.
feel: **Relieved** about the technology, irritated by constant money calculations.
S0.quote: The AI voice on my phone does not know whether the old plaster will crumble when I lift a skirting board.
fieldNote: Grace uses AI **daily** as a reference, but tests its answers against manuals and experienced workers.
Her own low pay becomes more important because Marc’s **injury** has made his driving hours irregular.

steps.text: Keep taking paid library repair shifts and checking measurements
Cancel the extra streaming subscription to pay van insurance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office may book and buy faster, but the library still needs someone to patch the actual wall. I would ask the supervisor to let the crew see the new schedule before it becomes an order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know my phone can already describe a repair, and a better system could give the supervisor an exact time for every job. I am a junior worker who sometimes needs help, so a target built for the quickest hand could cost me hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the new booking screen with the site lead this month and check where it records unexpected repairs. In the first year I would keep taking paid patching shifts and offer to photograph hidden damage for the site record, if the supervisor pays for that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel interested in the better records and wary of the clock. A photograph can show a rotten joist; it cannot make that joist safe in ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put on a damage record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would photograph the exposed timber beside a ruler, date it, and mark which room it came from. I already do a rough version in my notebook, so the screen could make it easier to hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you respond to an unrealistic target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the supervisor the photo and the extra time it took, then ask the crew to back me up. I am willing to use the system, but I would not hide a loose board to meet a number.

say: I would say **faster bookings** still leave walls for people to repair.
I would ask to **see schedules** before new targets are imposed.
think: I worry **timed repairs** could penalize the slower junior hands.
My **paid hours** might shrink even before robots can hold a tool.
do: Learn the **booking screen** with the site lead this month.
Keep taking **paid patching shifts** in the first year.
Photograph **hidden damage** for the record only if that time is paid.
feel: **Interested** in records, wary of unfair timing.
S1.quote: A photograph can show a rotten joist; it cannot make that joist safe in ten minutes.
fieldNote: Grace’s appetite for tools comes with a **pay condition**: recording damage must count as paid site time.
She connects **AI scheduling** to pressure on a junior worker’s pace, even while patching stays physical.

steps.text: Learn the new AI booking screen with the site lead
Keep taking paid library patching shifts
Ask the crew to back a challenge to unrealistic repair targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the thinking machine in 2028 could run the whole repair schedule, but we would still hold the tools until around 2031. I would ask to try its inspection guide in a real room and record where it is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 in 2028, and the office might reduce our visits if it trusts remote checks too much. At 63 in 2031, capable robots could patch walls and lift boards, which puts my low-paid place on the crew at risk while Marc is still uncertain about driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start saving dated photographs of my finished repairs now and ask the supervisor for a reference while the library contract runs. In 2029 I would apply to the local housing association for paid repair visits while keeping my site shifts; when robots arrive in 2031 I would ask my sister if her small hardware shop has paid counter hours, though I know a counter could change too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed, but I would start moving because waiting would make the rent problem worse. Two years will pass in about the time it takes this library to approve a change order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why move toward another repair employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The housing association has more than one building, so a paid vacancy might give me steadier weeks for now. I would not call repairs safe once the robots can do them; I would apply because we need wages before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Marc say about changing work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Marc says to ask for the reference before the contract ends, and he is right about that. His shoulder may heal or may keep cutting his driving shifts, so neither of us can promise the other a rescue.

say: I would say **thinking AI** can run schedules before robots handle repairs.
I would ask to **test guides** against a real room and record mistakes.
think: At **60**, remote checks could reduce visits even before physical robots arrive.
At **63**, capable robots could take my repair tasks while Marc’s earnings remain uncertain.
do: Collect **dated repair photos** and ask the supervisor for a reference now.
Apply for **housing association** repair visits in 2029 while keeping site shifts.
Ask my **sister’s shop** about paid counter hours if robots replace repairs.
feel: **Alarmed**, but ready to make applications before the rent is at risk.
S2.quote: Two years will pass in about the time it takes this library to approve a change order.
fieldNote: Grace plans around the **2028 office impact** and the later 2031 robot threat to her hands-on tasks.
Her housing application and hardware inquiry are **wage searches**, not claims that those jobs remain secure.

steps.text: Keep taking paid library site shifts through 2029
Apply for paid housing association repair visits in 2029
Ask her sister about paid hardware counter hours if robots replace repairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives workers a chance to collect proof of what we can do and try new equipment while we still have an employer. I would push for the contractor to pay for practice time rather than call it a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, planning and checks might be entirely automated, but I could still earn on physical repairs. At 66 in 2034, robots could do those repairs too, and I do not know what retirement income Marc and I would actually have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the site lead now to train me on the AI-assisted powered measuring rig and record the repairs I finish without a callback. In 2032 I would keep paid repair shifts and apply for a building maintenance vacancy at the college; before robots arrive I would ask the trade school about evening electrical-safety training if the fees are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel more capable with five years, although I cannot predict where the paid work will be. I want an employer to see a worker who can learn, not just my birth year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would electrical safety remain human work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know if an electrical-safety checker survives full AI and robots; the course could still help me earn during the warning years. I would not pay fees from the rent money for a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as useful training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want supervised practice with actual testers and a certificate the college accepts. A video and a quiz alone would not teach me what to do with a damaged socket.

say: I would ask for **paid practice** on new equipment during the warning years.
I would say a worker’s **repair record** should count alongside age.
think: At **63**, physical repair wages may continue after planning is automated.
At **66**, robots could end those wages before our retirement income is clear.
do: Practise the **powered measuring rig** with the site lead now.
Apply for **college maintenance** work in 2032 while staying on paid repairs.
Enroll in **electrical-safety training** if its fees are covered.
feel: **Capable**, yet uncertain where wages will come from after robots.
S3.quote: I want an employer to see a worker who can learn, not just my birth year.
fieldNote: Grace uses the longer lead time for **measured skill evidence** and a supervised equipment trial.
Her proposed **electrical-safety course** depends on funded fees and is not presented as a safe post-robot occupation.

steps.text: Practise the AI-assisted powered measuring rig with the site lead
Keep taking paid repair shifts in 2032
Apply for a college maintenance vacancy in 2032
Enroll in electrical-safety training only if course fees are covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say ten years is enough to make plans in the open rather than whisper about who gets dropped from the crew. I would ask the contractor to show older workers the same new tools it shows apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may choose shorter weeks if my knees allow, but I cannot assume we can pay bills without my wage. At 71 in 2039, robots may do every physical repair I do; the question is whether we have built a cushion by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid site work and set aside the money from one Saturday shift each month for a household reserve if the shifts exist. In 2037 I would test the new repair scanner with the site lead, review our real bills with Marc, and apply for any part-time college maintenance opening while I can still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel cautious hope, mostly because I could make a decision with numbers in front of us. A ten-year warning is only a gift if the wages keep arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own rent and families, and I would not put their income in our household column. We might ask for help in an emergency, but planning on it would be unfair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to stop site work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the reserve and Marc’s actual driving income with rent, food and insurance for several months. If they cover it, I could reduce shifts; if not, I would keep asking for paid work I can safely do.

say: I would ask for **equal tool access** for older workers and apprentices.
I would say **ten years** lets the crew talk openly about future shifts.
think: At **68**, shorter weeks may depend on money as much as my knees.
At **71**, capable robots could end physical repairs unless we have a real cushion.
do: Keep taking **paid site work** and save one Saturday wage monthly when possible.
Test the **repair scanner** with the site lead in 2037.
Apply for **part-time college maintenance** openings while able to work.
feel: **Cautious hope** grounded in actual wage and bill figures.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is only a gift if the wages keep arriving.
fieldNote: Grace refuses to treat grown children’s wages as a **retirement plan**, despite strong family ties.
She sees **2037 work and savings** as necessary before making any choice to reduce hours.

steps.text: Keep taking paid site work during 2037
Save one Saturday shift wage monthly when shifts exist
Test the AI repair scanner with the site lead in 2037
Apply for part-time college maintenance openings in 2037
